Lessons.Title: Rectangles with the Same Area
ExplanationParagraphs: This authored first-party lesson is aligned against the original 2021 IM K–5 Grade 3 Unit 7 Lesson 12: teacher lesson and preparation, all FOUR original pupil PDF pages, Activity 1’s small dot grid, the separate standard square dot paper from the original blackline master, and the section summary illustrated rectangles. Publisher images stay linked, not embedded. Gated original Cool-down Area of 36 not read or copied.

The source goal is to draw rectangles of equal area but differing perimeter (3.MD.D.8, 3.OA.C.7), reversing the comparison in the previous lesson. Source lesson schedule: mental Number Talk 10 minutes; Area of 24 15; Same Area, Different Perimeter 20; synthesis 10; original gated Cool-down 5. Original MLR8 discussion plus accessibility support for fine motor skills and peer explanation are teacher-directed.
Original warm-up is 40÷4=10, 60÷4=15, 80÷4=20, 96÷4=24. Quotient decomposition explains 96÷4 by (80÷4)+(16÷4)=20+4=24. Graded numeric responses are not a replacement for oral strategy.

Original Activity 12.1 page 2 asks pupils to DRAW AS MANY different rectangles on the printed dot grid as they can with AREA 24 square units and then find every perimeter. Ignoring rotation, positive-integer dimensions are 1×24 (P50), 2×12 (P28), 3×8 (P22), 4×6 (P20) linear grid units. The first 1×24 cannot fit the SHORTER dot grid printed directly on source page 2; that is a valid theoretical factor pair on the separate full-size standard dot paper, not proof it was drawn on source page 2. The 2×12, 3×8 and 4×6 rectangles can be drawn on that smaller grid. Do not require impossible diagrams just to claim exhaustiveness.

Original Activity 12.2 page 3 asks for TWO different rectangles each having the same AREA but DIFFERENT perimeters for targets 12, 20, 42 and 48 SQUARE units, plus a student-chosen fifth area. The teacher supplies standard square dot paper, 20 columns ×25 rows (19×24 grid-unit intervals). All drawn dimensions must fit this actual printable grid in either orientation. Typed proposals only validate possible dimensions; actual source sketches and cut-out activities remain teacher-checked.

Feasible example dimension pairs on the full-size 19×24 dot paper: area12: 2×6 (perimeter16) and 3×4 (perimeter14); area20: 2×10 (perimeter24) and 4×5 (perimeter18); area42: 3×14 (perimeter34) and 6×7 (perimeter26); area48: 4×12 (perimeter32) and 6×8 (perimeter28). Every pair has the same square-unit product but a DIFFERENT linear perimeter. 1×48 and 2×24 theoretically have area48; 1×48 does not fit source standard dot paper, while 2×24 can fit when rotated to put the long edge vertically.

Section Summary source page 4 visually confirms two distinct comparison families: one illustration groups rectangles with perimeter 16 and areas 7,12,15,16, while the other groups area-24 rectangles with perimeters 28,20,22. These source summary figures are not confused with the independent original 12.1 student drawing condition.

Source physical activity requires students to cut out rectangles, tape them to one of FOUR wall displays labeled 12,20,42,48 square units, and perform a partner gallery walk where they state a notice and a wonder. Students also choose their own area as fifth target. A numerical rectangle-pair checker cannot certify cutting, placement, cooperation, or discussion, and all physical tasks remain teacher-reviewed.

The critical contrast is area=a×b SQUARE units and perimeter=2(a+b) LINEAR units. Same products do not imply equal sums; orientation changes alone do not make a second different rectangle. Original publisher Cool-down remains gated, tests and Stage D have not been executed, publication and academic approval are not claimed.
The original 1×24 length-and-width option and source target areas 12, 20, 42 and 48 require teacher-gated review of actual same-area, different-perimeter rectangle drawings on the original dot grid.

KeyConcepts.Title: Area factor pairs
KeyConcepts.Definition: Rectangles have equal area when side products match.

KeyConcepts.Title: Perimeter may differ
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different factors can have different sums.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For equal area, require 2(a+b) not equal to 2(c+d).

KeyConcepts.Title: Grid bounds
KeyConcepts.Definition: Source standard square dot paper includes 19×24 intervals.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Both positive integer dimensions must fit in either orientation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Source 24-square-unit family
KeyConcepts.Example: Page-2 shorter printed grid cannot display 1×24 without changing paper.

WorkedExamples.Title: Same area 12
WorkedExamples.Question: Find two rectangles of area12 but different perimeter.
Steps: Compare equal product and different side sums.

WorkedExamples.Title: Area of 24
WorkedExamples.Question: How can source area24 have distinct perimeters?
WorkedExamples.Answer: Area24 with three different perimeter results

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Product and side sum are different quantities.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Accept two rotated copies of same rectangle.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Require DISTINCT PERIMETERS, not just visual orientation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Count a theoretical 1×48 rectangle as a source-grid drawing.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The full original paper has at most 24 continuous intervals vertically.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use dimension pairs physically fitting the grid.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat typed side lengths as full participation in poster/gallery activity.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The physical drawing and reasoning remain unevaluated.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Require teacher review of student work.

SummaryPoints: Source area24 families 1×24/P50,2×12/P28,3×8/P22,4×6/P20 (page2 grid too short for 1×24).
Source activity areas12,20,42,48 plus own choice, each requiring different PERIMETERS.
Physical cut-outs, posters, gallery walk and original gated Cool-down never automatically certified.
